clue.text: Academic carrying so many papers? That won’t happen

indicators.note: Someone carrying a load has it about their person, so the word that carries holds the other one inside it.

blocks.note: a don is a university teacher, the Oxbridge word for an academic
a ream is five hundred sheets of paper, sold and counted as one block

explanation.surface: A professor struggling along under a mountain of exam scripts.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter admitting that 'so many' is a quantity rather than a number, which is how a ream gets named without being named. Dons are the crossword's standard academics.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Dream on' is what you say to someone whose hope is pure fantasy — a flat way of telling them it will not be happening.

clue.text: Visit to fall through

blocks.note: to drop is to fall
you climb in by the window, meaning through it — 'by' in its sense of via

explanation.surface: A planned visit that ends up collapsing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall through' is one idiom on the surface and two separate words in the wordplay, and the split is the whole solve. 'By' meaning through is the sense in 'by way of'.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop by is to call in on somebody briefly and without ceremony, which is a visit.

clue.text: Entice hospital department to take blame

blocks.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat clinic, the department signposted in every British hospital
to take the rap is to accept the blame for something

explanation.surface: A hospital unit being lined up to carry the blame for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are set phrases rather than single words: the clinic is always initialised, and blame only becomes three letters through the idiom about taking it.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrap is to lure somebody in with a snare waiting at the end — enticement is the luring half of it.

clue.text: Unusual shop near me promoting unsophisticated stuff for lads

indicators.note: Something unusual is not as it usually is, and for a run of letters that means not in its usual order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: An odd little shop down the road pushing laddish tat.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder hides by reading as something else entirely — 'shop near me' is what you type into a search engine. The word defined is recent enough that the letter count is the safest way in.
explanation.definitionFit: The manosphere is the sprawl of websites, forums and podcasts selling macho grievance to young men: aimed at lads, and nobody's idea of sophisticated.

clue.text: Assassin employed by henchman in Japan

indicators.note: Somebody employed by a firm works away inside it, and these letters are at work inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: five letters running consecutively across the two gaps between these words

explanation.surface: A hired killer on the payroll of somebody's right-hand man in Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: The dominant false path is reading 'in Japan' as part of the definition, so the assassin is a Japanese one; it is not, because those letters are needed to finish the run.
explanation.definitionFit: A ninja was the covert agent of feudal Japan, trained in stealth and hired to kill — an assassin by trade.

clue.text: Boss put off at small transport hub

indicators.note: Milk goes off when it is no longer as it should be, and letters that have gone off are out of their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: The boss being dropped off at a modest little interchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put off' reads as one phrasal verb — dropped off, or discouraged — and the clue needs it prised apart, with 'put' joining the fodder and 'off' doing the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus stop is the smallest piece of public transport infrastructure there is: a named place where a service calls and passengers change.

clue.text: Threaten to boycott post?

blocks.note: to black goods is British trade-union language for refusing to handle them, which is a boycott
the post and the mail are the same delivery

explanation.surface: A threat to stop the letters getting through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black' as a verb is union vocabulary: a blacked cargo is one nobody will touch. The question mark is the setter conceding that threatening the postal service is not what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: To blackmail is to threaten someone with exposure unless they pay, so the bare verb 'threaten' is the heart of the crime.

clue.text: Star Trek occasionally will meet expectations

indicators.note: What happens occasionally happens every so often rather than every time, so only every other letter is taken.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of these two words, counted straight through the space

explanation.surface: Star Trek living up to what its fans want of it now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: To sate is to satisfy something to the full — the verb buried inside 'insatiable'. The surface's joke is a fan's: a series that only occasionally delivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sating a hunger means satisfying it completely, so what was expected of the meal has been met rather than half met.

clue.text: Display ambition to make weak king great

blocks.note: a thin argument or a thin excuse is a weak one
K is the king on a playing card and in chess notation
a big name is a great one

explanation.surface: A feeble monarch being talked up into a great one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weak king' reads as one idea, and that is what hides the seam: the first two pieces fuse into a word of their own before 'great' arrives to finish the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To think big is to set your sights high — ambition shown in the scale of what is planned rather than in anything achieved yet.

clue.text: Main gaps teased out in naturalistic religion

indicators.note: Teasing out a tangle pulls the strands loose and lays them down in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Somebody picking apart the big holes in a nature-worshipping faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main gaps' looks like the subject of a sentence about a religion's weaknesses and is the raw material instead. Pagan faiths take their gods and festivals from the turning seasons, which is what 'naturalistic' points at.
explanation.definitionFit: Paganism covers the pre-Christian and revived nature religions, whose worship is organised around the land and the year rather than a revealed book.

clue.text: Work can provide way to participate

definitions.note: 'Opt in' is a verb phrase while 'way to participate' names a thing; the setter leans on the noun form that pension schemes and mailing lists have made familiar — an opt-in.

blocks.note: op is the composer's opus, the numbered work on a score
a tin of beans is a can of them

explanation.surface: A job offering a route into something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the verb holding the sentence together and is a container on a shelf. Op for work comes off concert programmes, where Op. 27 is the twenty-seventh piece a composer published.
explanation.definitionFit: To opt in is to say yes to taking part — the choice that puts you inside a scheme, where opting out leaves you outside it.

clue.text: Pole making current safe – it was touch and go

definitions.note: 'Touch and go' is an adjective phrase and the answer is a noun, but the idioms swap whole: it was touch and go, it was a near thing.

blocks.note: the north pole, N on any compass
earthing a circuit runs a wire to ground so stray current cannot hurt anybody

explanation.surface: An electrician earthing a live pole in a job that almost went wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter offers a Warsaw native and the clue means the compass point, which is the trap here. Earthing is the British electrician's word for the safety connection Americans call grounding.
explanation.definitionFit: A near thing is an outcome that came within an inch of going the other way — precisely the precariousness 'touch and go' describes.

clue.text: Underwear, piles of it, is fundamental stuff

blocks.note: the commonest item of women's underwear, in the plural the clue's comma asks for
a pile of plates is a stack of them
surface only — it keeps the picture of a heap of lingerie and contributes no letters

explanation.surface: A drawer with heaps of underwear crammed into it.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces do not break where the answer breaks: the S that ends the first also begins the second, and the enumeration puts the split one letter later than the wordplay does.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting down to brass tacks means getting past the talk to the basic facts, so brass tacks are the fundamentals of a matter.

clue.text: It’s like being a family member

blocks.note: the article taken exactly as it stands
your kin are your family collectively, and a single one of them is a member of it

explanation.surface: What it feels like to be one of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the clue's own words run together, which is what makes it hard to see — you have read past it before you have finished the sentence. It is normally met as 'akin to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Akin means like or similar: something akin to a thing is of the same kind as it.

clue.text: There’s nothing more to read – and that’s that

blocks.note: the last page of a book, with white paper below the final line
the sentence that closes an argument and refuses to reopen it

explanation.surface: Somebody shutting a book and declining to discuss it any further.
explanation.walkthrough: One phrase, two lives: the literal one belongs to a book, the idiomatic one to an argument. The dash in the middle is the setter marking the seam between them.
explanation.definitionFit: You reach the end of a story when there is nothing left on the page; said flatly to somebody, the same words mean the matter is closed.

clue.text: Tough calls upset Sandra inside

indicators.note: Upsetting something tips it over and spills what was in it out of order.
What is inside a word sits between its outer parts, so one piece is planted in the middle of the other.

blocks.note: to hail a taxi is to call it
the six letters of the name, upset into a new order

explanation.surface: Difficult decisions leaving Sandra quietly distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tough calls' reads as one phrase — hard decisions — and the clue needs it split, with the calls becoming shouts across a street. The name then goes in after the first letter only, which is the awkward part.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody hard as nails feels nothing and gives nothing away: the idiom takes toughness as far as it goes.

clue.text: Contact dealer in illegal stuff to isolate funds

blocks.note: to ring somebody is to contact them by telephone
a fence is the receiver who buys stolen goods and passes them on

explanation.surface: Phoning a crook who trades in contraband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contact' looks like a noun — the underworld contact the surface wants — and is a verb. The answer's own picture is agricultural: money penned into a field of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring-fence a budget is to wall it off so nothing else can be spent from it, which is isolating the money.

clue.text: Big pots made from sticks?

blocks.note: a pot in this sense is a paunch, the belly that hangs over a belt
British colloquial for putting up with something: he can't stick it

explanation.surface: Large containers woven out of sticks.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves have to be plural to work, so the second is the verb in its he-does-it form rather than the noun. The question mark covers a surface in which nothing is actually made from anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Stomachs are bellies, big ones in the pot sense; and to stomach something is to endure it, just as sticking it does.

clue.text: Tension in bad housing is never ending

indicators.note: To house something is to give it a place inside, so the word doing the housing closes around the other.

blocks.note: bad in the moral sense, of conduct rather than quality
T is the physicist's symbol for the tension in a rope or wire

explanation.surface: The strain of life in substandard housing, with no end to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad housing' reads as one phrase and is two instructions: the bad is a word in its own right, and the housing is what to do with it. Wickedness, not poor quality, is the sense that spells out.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immortal cannot die, so its existence has no ending to arrive at.

clue.text: Plain merlot mixed up with another red

indicators.note: Mixing wines, or letters, throws them together in no particular order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: An unremarkable merlot being blended with a second red.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the first two words entire, and the enumeration matches their letter count exactly, which is the quickest confirmation available. One grape is named openly and the other has to be assembled.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempranillo is the black grape behind Rioja and Ribera del Duero, and the wine made from it — another red to set beside the merlot.

clue.text: Spill the beans on party matter

blocks.note: a do is a party or function — the office do, a big do on Saturday
to tell is to count or have an effect: every blow told, age tells in the end

explanation.surface: Informing on something that happened at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell' meaning to have an effect is the older sense, and it is what 'matter' reaches for. The definition is an invitation rather than an order, which the imperative surface disguises.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Do tell' is the standing invitation to somebody sitting on gossip: out with it, let us have the beans.

clue.text: Lean place to stay in channel

indicators.note: 'In' puts what comes before it inside what comes after it.

blocks.note: Sky is a British television broadcaster, so a channel you watch rather than one you sail
an inn is somewhere to put up for the night

explanation.surface: A narrow little guesthouse beside a stretch of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' offers water and means television, and 'lean' has to be the adjective rather than the verb the surface hands you. The broadcaster's three letters sit round the lodging.
explanation.definitionFit: Skinny means lean to the point of being underweight — thin with nothing spare on the frame.

clue.text: Expose rear of satellite?

blocks.note: the student prank of dropping the trousers and presenting the backside
a body in orbit round a planet rather than round the sun

explanation.surface: Uncovering the back end of a spacecraft.
explanation.walkthrough: The false path is a good one: 'rear of satellite' looks exactly like an instruction to take a last letter. It is nothing of the kind — the two senses simply sit next to each other and the question mark flags the join.
explanation.definitionFit: To moon is to bare your backside at somebody; a moon is a natural satellite, ours being the one everybody means.

clue.text: Dessert wine gets another shake

blocks.note: afters is the British table word for the pudding course
hock is the English name for German white wine from the Rhine

explanation.surface: A sweet wine given another shake before it is poured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dessert wine' reads as one item on a list and has to break in two. Both halves are old British table talk: afters is what follows the main course, hock what the Victorians drank with it.
explanation.definitionFit: An aftershock is the lesser tremor that follows an earthquake — the same ground shaken a second time.

clue.text: Do well calling out extra large letters

indicators.note: Calling something out is saying it aloud, so what counts is the noise it makes and not how it is written.

blocks.note: XL is the size printed on a shirt label for extra large; the two letters are named one after the other

explanation.surface: Shouting out the letters printed extra large.
explanation.walkthrough: XL is the size on a garment label and the crossword's shorthand for extra large. Naming those two letters aloud is the whole mechanism, and the spelling that comes out has a C in it that nobody said.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel is to do notably well — to stand out above the ordinary standard rather than merely meet it.

clue.text: Surprise at temperature within star

indicators.note: What sits within something is held between its outer parts.

blocks.note: our own star, the one overhead every day
T is the standard abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: Astonishment at how hot a star runs.
explanation.walkthrough: When a clue wants a short star, the one in our own sky is the first to try — celebrities come later. The surface's astonishment is doing the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: To stun somebody is to surprise them so completely that they cannot react at all.

clue.text: Unresponsive pet perhaps needs a pick-me-up

blocks.note: 'perhaps' marks this as one example of a pet rather than the word for all of them
the article taken exactly as it stands
a tonic is the drink or medicine taken to perk somebody up

explanation.surface: A listless pet that could do with something to buck it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the fairness signal: without it the setter would be offering one breed of pet as the word for pets in general. The medical sense is real — catatonia is a state of frozen stillness.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody catatonic is rigid and unreacting, the clinical word for a total failure to respond to what is going on.

clue.text: Poem about film theatre

blocks.note: an ode is a poem addressed to its subject
a book on birds is a book about birds

explanation.surface: A poem written about the local cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is the trap: nine times in ten it tells you to put one thing round another, and here it is two letters of its own. The Greek odeion was a roofed hall for song before the name went up over British cinemas.
explanation.definitionFit: An odeon is a cinema — the name of the chain that put picture palaces on British high streets in the 1930s.

clue.text: Scottish extremists call quietly for it?

definitions.text: Scottish extremists call quietly for it?

blocks.note: on the surface, hardliners at the edges of Scottish politics; in the wordplay, the two letters at the extreme ends of the word 'Scottish'
those two end letters read as a word are SH, which is what a librarian says and never a loud thing to say

explanation.surface: Scottish hardliners making a discreet demand for something.
explanation.walkthrough: No letters change hands here. The clue works by getting you to say the extremes of 'Scottish' out loud: SH is both what they spell and what you do to a noisy room.
explanation.definitionFit: SH is the universal call for quiet, so what those two letters are quietly asking for is the hush the answer names.

clue.text: Young Adult fiction collects money in a very reliable way

indicators.note: To collect something is to gather it in, so one piece closes around the other — loosely used here, since it is the money that does the gathering rather than the fiction.

blocks.note: lolly is British slang for cash
YA is the publishing trade's label for the Young Adult shelf, taken from the initials

explanation.surface: Teen novels bringing in the cash, dependably.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion runs the opposite way to the clue's grammar: the slang for money closes around the initials, not the other way about. Solvers complained about that on the day, and they were right to.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting loyally is acting with steady allegiance, which is reliability of the kind that means somebody will not switch sides.
